```{=html}
<div class="title-block-inner">
```

# The problem {.dark-slide background-image="assets/slide-frame-dark.png" background-size="cover" background-color="#031042"}

```{=html}
<div class="eyebrow">Grid search</div>
```

- Tuning is embarrassingly parallel, and embarrassingly slow

- The hardware you tune on is rarely the hardware you have

## A small grid is a lot of fitting {background-image="assets/slide-frame.png" background-size="cover" background-color="white"}

```{=html}
<div class="eyebrow">Grid search</div>
```

- A boosted tree with four tuning parameters: `mtry`, `min_n`, `learn_rate`, `tree_depth`

- A space filling grid of **100 combinations**

- 10 fold cross validation

:::{.stat}
1,000
:::

:::{.stat-sub}
model fits for one call to `tune_grid()`
:::

## The usual answers fall short {background-image="assets/slide-frame.png" background-size="cover" background-color="white"}

```{=html}
<div class="eyebrow">Grid search</div>
```

- Run it in parallel on your laptop, and you are bound by the cores you own

- Move it to a server, and the server is often *slower* than the laptop

- Rewrite the model in Spark ML, and you leave tidymodels behind

- Meanwhile the Databricks cluster your data already lives in sits idle

# The example {.dark-slide background-image="assets/slide-frame-dark.png" background-size="cover" background-color="#031042"}

```{=html}
<div class="eyebrow">The example</div>
```

- Hospital readmissions, a plain tidymodels workflow

- Nothing in it is written for Spark

## Splits and recipe {background-image="assets/slide-frame.png" background-size="cover" background-color="white"}

```{=html}
<div class="eyebrow">The example</div>
```

:::{.sample-small}
```r
library(tidymodels)
library(readmission)

set.seed(231)
readmission_splits <- initial_split(readmission, strata = readmitted)

readmission_folds <- vfold_cv(training(readmission_splits), strata = readmitted)

recipe_basic <- recipe(readmitted ~ ., data = training(readmission_splits)) |>
  step_mutate(
    race = factor(case_when(
      !(race %in% c("Caucasian", "African American")) ~ "Other",
      .default = race
    ))
  ) |>
  step_unknown(all_nominal_predictors()) |>
  step_YeoJohnson(all_numeric_predictors()) |>
  step_normalize(all_numeric_predictors()) |>
  step_dummy(all_nominal_predictors())
```
:::

## Model and grid {background-image="assets/slide-frame.png" background-size="cover" background-color="white"}

```{=html}
<div class="eyebrow">The example</div>
```

:::{.sample-small}
```r
spec_bt <- boost_tree(
  mode = "classification",
  trees = 500,
  mtry = tune(),
  min_n = tune(),
  learn_rate = tune(),
  tree_depth = tune()
)

bt_grid <- grid_space_filling(
  mtry(range = c(5, 20)),
  min_n(),
  learn_rate(),
  tree_depth(),
  size = 100
)
```
:::

## Tuning locally {background-image="assets/slide-frame.png" background-size="cover" background-color="white"}

```{=html}
<div class="eyebrow">The example</div>
```

:::{.sample-small}
```r
library(future)
plan(multisession)

local_results <- tune_grid(
  object = spec_bt,
  preprocessor = recipe_basic,
  resamples = readmission_folds,
  grid = bt_grid,
  control = control_grid()
)
```
:::

:::{.fragment .fade-in}
An M3 laptop takes **11 minutes**. A Windows machine takes **61**.
:::

# tune_grid_spark() {.dark-slide background-image="assets/slide-frame-dark.png" background-size="cover" background-color="#031042"}

```{=html}
<div class="eyebrow">The feature</div>
```

- Same tidymodels objects, fitted on Databricks workers

- One extra argument, and nothing else changes

## One new argument {background-image="assets/slide-frame.png" background-size="cover" background-color="white"}

```{=html}
<div class="eyebrow">The feature</div>
```

:::{.sample-small}
```r
library(sparklyr)

sc <- spark_connect(
  method = "databricks_connect",
  cluster_id = cluster_id
)

spark_results <- tune_grid_spark(
  sc = sc,                          # the only addition
  object = spec_bt,
  preprocessor = recipe_basic,
  resamples = readmission_folds,
  grid = bt_grid,
  control = control_grid(verbose = TRUE)
)
```
:::

- It returns a regular `tune_results` object, so `collect_metrics()` and `select_best()` work as usual

## What happens under the hood {background-image="assets/slide-frame.png" background-size="cover" background-color="white"}

```{=html}
<div class="eyebrow">The feature</div>
```

```{=html}
<div class="cards">
  <div class="card">
    <h3>Upload</h3>
    <p>The resamples, the model specification and the preprocessing steps are serialized and sent to Databricks.</p>
  </div>
  <div class="card">
    <h3>Process</h3>
    <p>Each parameter combination is fitted on a worker, running real R through <code>reticulate</code> and <code>rpy2</code>.</p>
  </div>
  <div class="card">
    <h3>Collect</h3>
    <p>The metrics come back and are assembled into a <code>tune_results</code> object.</p>
  </div>
</div>
```

## Preparing the cluster, once {background-image="assets/slide-frame.png" background-size="cover" background-color="white"}

```{=html}
<div class="eyebrow">The feature</div>
```

:::{.sample-small}
```r
repo <- "https://databricks.packagemanager.posit.co/cran/__linux__/noble/latest"

r_libs <- libraries(
  lib_cran("reticulate", repo = repo),
  lib_cran("tidymodels", repo = repo),
  lib_cran("xgboost", repo = repo),
  lib_cran("readmission", repo = repo)
)

db_libs_install(cluster_id, r_libs)

py_lib <- lib_pypi("rpy2==3.5.7") |>
  libraries()

db_libs_install(cluster_id, py_lib)

wait_for_lib_installs(cluster_id)
```
:::

- Scripted with `brickster`, or done by hand in the cluster's Libraries tab

# The payoff {.dark-slide background-image="assets/slide-frame-dark.png" background-size="cover" background-color="#031042"}

```{=html}
<div class="eyebrow">The payoff</div>
```

- The same 100 combinations, run in five places

## Time to tune 100 combinations {background-image="assets/slide-frame.png" background-size="cover" background-color="white"}

```{=html}
<div class="eyebrow">The payoff</div>
```

```{=html}
<div class="bench">
  <div class="row"><div class="label">Spark, 32 concurrent</div><div class="bar fast" style="width:19px"></div><div class="time">2.8 min</div></div>
  <div class="row"><div class="label">Spark, 10 concurrent</div><div class="bar fast" style="width:35px"></div><div class="time">5 min</div></div>

```

## What the numbers say {background-image="assets/slide-frame.png" background-size="cover" background-color="white"}

```{=html}
<div class="eyebrow">The payoff</div>
```

- **32x faster** than the same job on Posit Workbench, **4x faster** than the best laptop

- Concurrency is a dial: 10 workers gave 5 minutes, 32 gave 2.8

- An overnight job becomes a job you wait for

- Faster tuning means larger grids, which means better models

# Knowing the limits {.dark-slide background-image="assets/slide-frame-dark.png" background-size="cover" background-color="#031042"}

```{=html}
<div class="eyebrow">Limits</div>
```

- What this is, and what it is not

## Limitations {background-image="assets/slide-frame.png" background-size="cover" background-color="white"}

```{=html}
<div class="eyebrow">Limits</div>
```

- The goal is to speed up the **search**, not to process big data. The data still has to fit in memory

- Results can differ slightly from local runs, because the OS, the R version and the package versions differ

- Downloading predictions roughly doubles the data moved across the wire

- If your data is larger than local memory, reach for Spark ML instead
